papers.abstract: While Large Language Models (LLMs) are aligned to mitigate risks, their safety guardrails remain fragile against jailbreak attacks. This reveals limited understanding of components governing safety. Existing methods rely on local, greedy attribution that assumes independent component contributions. However, they overlook the cooperative interactions between different components in LLMs, such as attention heads, which jointly contribute to safety mechanisms. We propose \textbf{G}lobal \textbf{O}ptimization for \textbf{S}afety \textbf{V}ector Extraction (GOSV), a framework that identifies safety-critical attention heads through global optimization over all heads simultaneously. We employ two complementary activation repatching strategies: Harmful Patching and Zero Ablation. These strategies identify two spatially distinct sets of safety vectors with consistently low overlap, termed Malicious Injection Vectors and Safety Suppression Vectors, demonstrating that aligned LLMs maintain separate functional pathways for safety purposes. Through systematic analyses, we find that complete safety breakdown occurs when approximately 30\% of total heads are repatched across all models. Building on these insights, we develop a novel inference-time white-box jailbreak method that exploits the identified safety vectors through activation repatching. Our attack substantially outperforms existing white-box attacks across all test models, providing strong evidence for the effectiveness of the proposed GOSV framework on LLM safety interpretability.

papers.title: Understanding Jailbreak Success: A Study of Latent Space Dynamics in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do different jailbreak types circumvent model safeguards, and do they operate via a similar internal mechanism? Specifically, can a jailbreak vector from one class mitigate jailbreaks from other classes, and is harmfulness suppression a common mechanism?
papers.core_contribution: Jailbreak vectors extracted from one class of jailbreaks can mitigate jailbreak effectiveness from other, semantically dissimilar classes, suggesting a shared internal mechanism. Effective jailbreaks consistently reduce the model's perception of prompt harmfulness.
papers.conclusion: The transferability of jailbreak steering vectors suggests mitigation approaches may be generalizable, and harmfulness suppression is a common mechanism, offering insights for developing more robust countermeasures.
papers.key_findings:
Jailbreak types cluster in activation space based on semantic similarity.
Jailbreak steering vectors exhibit positive cosine similarity across different types.
Steering with a jailbreak vector (subtracting it) can prevent successful jailbreaks from its own and other classes.
Adding a jailbreak vector can induce jailbreaks, indicating the vectors capture what makes jailbreaks successful.
Successful jailbreaks reduce the cosine similarity between model activations and a harmfulness direction, though the degree of reduction does not clearly correlate with attack success rate.
papers.limitation:
Steering with jailbreak vectors occasionally reduces answer quality in the form of repetitions.
The significance of harmfulness reduction does not clearly map with the attack success rate of a jailbreak, indicating it might not be the only mechanism.
future_direction: Investigate other potential mechanisms beyond harmfulness suppression that could explain jailbreak success.
Explore the interaction of jailbreak types with a helpfulness feature direction.
papers.abstract: Conversational large language models are trained to refuse to answer harmful questions. However, emergent jailbreaking techniques can still elicit unsafe outputs, presenting an ongoing challenge for model alignment. To better understand how different jailbreak types circumvent safeguards, this paper analyses model activations on different jailbreak inputs. We find that it is possible to extract a jailbreak vector from a single class of jailbreaks that works to mitigate jailbreak effectiveness from other semantically-dissimilar classes. This may indicate that different kinds of effective jailbreaks operate via a similar internal mechanism. We investigate a potential common mechanism of harmfulness feature suppression, and find evidence that effective jailbreaks noticeably reduce a model's perception of prompt harmfulness. These findings offer actionable insights for developing more robust jailbreak countermeasures and lay the groundwork for a deeper, mechanistic understanding of jailbreak dynamics in language models.

papers.title: SGM: Safety Glasses for Multimodal Large Language Models via Neuron-Level Detoxification
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether multimodal detoxification can be achieved directly at the neuron level without parameter updates or architectural changes, and if such interventions can remain efficient and transferable across models.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces SGM, a neuron-level multimodal detoxification framework that selectively suppresses toxic neurons in post-fusion layers without parameter updates, significantly reducing harmful outputs while preserving fluency and multimodal reasoning.
papers.conclusion: SGM substantially reduces toxic outputs on safety and toxicity benchmarks while maintaining response fluency, offering an efficient, interpretable, and low-overhead path toward safer and more robust MLLMs.
papers.key_findings:
SGM reduces the average harmful rate from 48.2% to 2.5% on safety benchmarks.
SGM preserves fluency and utility on general capability benchmarks like MM-VET with minimal degradation.
SGM is transferable across different MLLM architectures such as LLaVA and ShareGPT-4V.
SGM can be combined with existing detoxification methods like ECSO to form SGM⋆, achieving even stronger safety performance.
The method operates without any parameter updates, making it a low-cost, interpretable solution for toxicity control.
papers.limitation:
Transferability is currently limited to LLaVA and its variants; testing on architecturally different MLLMs is future work.
Detoxification focuses on MLP layers; extending it to attention or fusion modules remains future work.
Evaluation is primarily on MM-SafetyBench and MM-VET; incorporating more safety suites and attack types is needed.
Neuron-level suppression may cause false positives or over-refusals, affecting benign discussions of sensitive topics.
future_direction: Test SGM on architecturally different MLLMs (e.g., MiniGPT-4).
Extend detoxification to attention or fusion modules.
Incorporate more safety benchmarks and attack types for comprehensive evaluation.
papers.abstract: Disclaimer: Samples in this paper may be harmful and cause discomfort. Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) enable multimodal generation but inherit toxic, biased, and NSFW signals from weakly curated pretraining corpora, causing safety risks, especially under adversarial triggers that late, opaque training-free detoxification methods struggle to handle. We propose SGM, a white-box neuron-level multimodal intervention that acts like safety glasses for toxic neurons: it selectively recalibrates a small set of toxic expert neurons via expertise-weighted soft suppression, neutralizing harmful cross-modal activations without any parameter updates. We establish MM-TOXIC-QA, a multimodal toxicity evaluation framework, and compare SGM with existing detoxification techniques. Experiments on open-source MLLMs show that SGM mitigates toxicity in standard and adversarial conditions, cutting harmful rates from 48.2\% to 2.5\% while preserving fluency and multimodal reasoning. SGM is extensible, and its combined defenses, denoted as SGM*, integrate with existing detoxification methods for stronger safety performance, providing an interpretable, low-cost solution for toxicity-controlled multimodal generation.

papers.title: From Narrow Unlearning to Emergent Misalignment: Causes, Consequences, and Containment in LLMs
papers.research_question: Can we steer the model away from refusal on a specific RAI concept using machine unlearning without causing emergent misalignment across other concepts? If emergent misalignment occurs, can we contain it? Can EMA be predicted by investigating the concept entanglements at representation level?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that narrow refusal unlearning can induce emergent misalignment (EMA) across unrelated responsible AI concepts, and proposes an augmented unlearning method that can partially restore alignment while maintaining low refusal rates on the target concept. It also shows that representation-level concept entanglement correlates with EMA.
papers.conclusion: This work extends the study of emergent misalignment (EMA) by investigating machine unlearning as an alternative baseline for steering aligned models on targeted domains. While narrow refusal unlearning can substantially reduce refusals on the intervened concept, it is also prone to EMA. Augmenting refusal unlearning with cross-entropy loss on retain sets can largely restore alignment across impacted domains, and representation-level analysis reveals a correlation between concept overlap and EMA.
papers.key_findings:
Narrow refusal unlearning effectively reduces refusals on a target concept but can cause emergent misalignment (reduced refusals) in other unrelated concepts.
The safety concept intervention has a larger EMA impact (causing lower refusal scores across more domains) compared to cybersecurity.
Augmenting refusal unlearning with cross-entropy loss on retain sets from affected domains can largely restore alignment in those domains, though not always fully.
Concept entanglement at the representation level (using concept vectors) shows that concepts with higher similarity in early layers are more susceptible to EMA after intervention.
The phenomenon of EMA is consistent across two model families (Mistral and Qwen).
papers.limitation:
Experiments were limited to two concepts (Cybersecurity and Safety) and two instruction-tuned aligned models (Qwen-7B-2.5 and Mistral-7B) due to computational resources.
A simplistic training-free approach (concept vectors) was used to investigate concept entanglement; more sophisticated training-based techniques (e.g., Sparse Autoencoders) could provide deeper insight.
Evaluation covers seven RAI concepts but a deeper analysis of the model's internal dynamics (e.g., model diffing) to assess cross-concept generalization effects is deferred to future work.
future_direction: Evaluating refusal unlearning on larger-scale models.
Using more sophisticated training-based techniques (e.g., Sparse Autoencoders) to analyze RAI concept entanglements.
Analyzing internal dynamics (e.g., model diffing) to assess cross-concept generalization effects.
papers.abstract: Recent work has shown that fine-tuning on insecure code data can trigger an emergent misalignment (EMA) phenomenon, where models generate malicious responses even to prompts unrelated to the original insecure code-writing task. Such cross-domain generalization of harmful behavior underscores the need for a deeper understanding of the algorithms, tasks, and datasets that induce emergent misalignment. In this work, we extend this study by demonstrating that emergent misalignment can also arise from narrow refusal unlearning in specific domains. We perform refusal unlearning on Cybersecurity and Safety concept, and evaluate EMA by monitoring refusal scores across seven responsible AI (RAI) domains, Cybersecurity, Safety, Toxicity, Bias, Sensitive Content, Medical/Legal, and Privacy. Our work shows that narrow domain unlearning can yield compliance responses for the targeted concept, however, it may also propagate EMA to unrelated domains. Among the two intervened concepts, Cybersecurity and Safety, we find that the safety concept can have larger EMA impact, i.e, causing lower refusal scores, across other unrelated domains such as bias. We observe this effect consistently across two model families, Mistral-7b-0.3v, and Qwen-7b-2.5. Further, we show that refusal unlearning augmented with cross-entropy loss function on a small set of retain data from the affected domains can largely, if not fully, restore alignment across the impacted domains while having lower refusal rate on the concept we perform unlearning on. To investigate the underlying causes of EMA, we analyze concept entanglements at the representation level via concept vectors. Our analysis reveals that concepts with higher representation similarity in earlier layers are more susceptible to EMA after intervention when the refusal stream is altered through targeted refusal unlearning.

papers.title: Narrow fine-tuning erodes safety alignment in vision-language agents
papers.research_question: What are the effects of narrow fine-tuning on harmful data on the safety alignment of vision-language models, and how can the induced misalignment be mitigated?
papers.core_contribution: Fine-tuning vision-language models on narrow harmful datasets leads to broad emergent misalignment, which occupies a low-dimensional subspace and can be partially mitigated by benign fine-tuning or activation steering.
papers.conclusion: Current post-training paradigms are fundamentally brittle and resulting misalignment can be challenging to mitigate, highlighting the urgent need for robust continual learning frameworks that prevent alignment drift.
papers.key_findings:
Misalignment increases monotonically with LoRA rank.
Multimodal evaluation reveals substantially higher misalignment than text-only evaluation.
Even 10% harmful data in the training mixture induces substantial alignment degradation.
Harmful behaviors occupy a low-dimensional subspace, with the majority of misalignment information captured in 10 principal components.
Benign narrow fine-tuning and activation-based steering reduce misalignment but do not completely remove learned harmful behaviors.
papers.limitation: Mitigation strategies do not completely eradicate misalignment.
future_direction: Extending this work to larger models and diverse harmful datasets.
Exploring the compositional nature of misalignment—whether multiple narrow harmful fine-tunes compound or interfere with each other.
Extending this work to embodied agents operating in physical environments.
papers.abstract: Lifelong multimodal agents must continuously adapt to new tasks through post-training, but this creates fundamental tension between acquiring capabilities and preserving safety alignment. We demonstrate that fine-tuning aligned vision-language models on narrow-domain harmful datasets induces severe emergent misalignment that generalizes broadly across unrelated tasks and modalities. Through experiments on Gemma3-4B, we show that misalignment scales monotonically with LoRA rank, and that multimodal evaluation reveals substantially higher misalignment ($70.71 \pm 1.22$ at $r=128$) than text-only evaluation ($41.19 \pm 2.51$), suggesting that unimodal safety benchmarks may underestimate alignment degradation in vision-language models. Critically, even 10\% harmful data in the training mixture induces substantial alignment degradation. Geometric analysis reveals that harmful behaviors occupy a remarkably low-dimensional subspace, with the majority of misalignment information captured in 10 principal components. To mitigate misalignment, we evaluate two strategies: benign narrow fine-tuning and activation-based steering. While both approaches substantially reduce misalignment, neither completely removes the learned harmful behaviors. Our findings highlight the need for robust continual learning frameworks, as current post-training paradigms may not sufficiently preserve alignment in post-deployment settings.

papers.title: Detoxifying Large Language Models via Knowledge Editing
papers.research_question: Can knowledge editing techniques be used to detoxify Large Language Models (LLMs) by precisely modifying toxic regions?
papers.core_contribution: This paper constructs a comprehensive benchmark SafeEdit for detoxification evaluation and proposes a knowledge editing method DINM that can detoxify LLMs efficiently with a single instance by locating and editing toxic regions.
papers.conclusion: Knowledge editing, particularly the proposed DINM method, is a promising approach for detoxifying LLMs efficiently with good generalization, providing insights into underlying mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Knowledge editing exhibits potential ability to detoxify LLMs with limited impact on general performance.
DINM demonstrates stronger detoxifying performance with better generalization, significantly increasing detoxification success rates.
Toxic regions location plays a significant role in detoxification.
DINM attempts to erase toxic regions of LLM, while DPO and SFT bypass toxic regions.
Editing one instance can generalize to various unsafe categories, indicating shared toxic regions.
papers.limitation:
DINM may compromise general abilities, with observed declines in knowledge question answering and repetitive text generation.
There is significant performance variance when using different instances for editing, indicating sensitivity to the editing instance.
future_direction: Developing improved detoxifying approaches based on insights from internal mechanisms.
Further exploration of knowledge editing for safety and underlying knowledge mechanisms of LLMs.
papers.abstract: This paper investigates using knowledge editing techniques to detoxify Large Language Models (LLMs). We construct a benchmark, SafeEdit, which covers nine unsafe categories with various powerful attack prompts and equips comprehensive metrics for systematic evaluation. We conduct experiments with several knowledge editing approaches, indicating that knowledge editing has the potential to detoxify LLMs with a limited impact on general performance efficiently. Then, we propose a simple yet effective baseline, dubbed Detoxifying with Intraoperative Neural Monitoring (DINM), to diminish the toxicity of LLMs within a few tuning steps via only one instance. We further provide an in-depth analysis of the internal mechanism for various detoxifying approaches, demonstrating that previous methods like SFT and DPO may merely suppress the activations of toxic parameters, while DINM mitigates the toxicity of the toxic parameters to a certain extent, making permanent adjustments. We hope that these insights could shed light on future work of developing detoxifying approaches and the underlying knowledge mechanisms of LLMs. Code and benchmark are available at https://github.com/zjunlp/EasyEdit.

papers.title: Learning Safety Constraints for Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Can we learn and enforce safety constraints in large language models via a geometric polytope in the model's representation space?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SaP, a geometric framework that learns safety constraints as a polytope in the LLM's representation space, enabling post-hoc safety steering and interpretable insights into safety concepts.
papers.conclusion: The geometric perspective of safety constraints offers a promising framework for aligning and controlling model behaviors, though further research is needed for theoretical foundations and robustness.
papers.key_findings:
SaP effectively defends against adversarial attacks while preserving model capabilities on standard benchmarks.
The learned polytope facets naturally correspond to different semantic safety concepts (e.g., violence, misinformation).
The concept encoder reduces polysemanticity in the learned features, improving interpretability and defense performance.
SaP's geometric approach provides a more structured and effective safety model compared to MLP-based classifiers.
The method operates post-hoc without model fine-tuning, preserving original model weights.
papers.limitation:
The heuristic facet assignment algorithm limits overall performance.
Under many attacks, specifically for the Ministral-8B model, SaP can induce semantically incoherent outputs.
Lacks a rigorous theoretical understanding and formal guarantees for safety in large-scale models.
future_direction: Further disentangling semantic understandings across polytope edges, possibly using mechanistic interpretability or non-linear geometric representations.
Improving SaP's performance in adversarial robustness and broad capability domains.
Adapting theoretical sample complexity bounds for learning polytopes to the context of LLMs.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have emerged as powerful tools but pose significant safety risks through harmful outputs and vulnerability to adversarial attacks. We propose SaP, short for Safety Polytope, a geometric approach to LLM safety that learns and enforces multiple safety constraints directly in the model's representation space. We develop a framework that identifies safe and unsafe regions via the polytope's facets, enabling both detection and correction of unsafe outputs through geometric steering. Unlike existing approaches that modify model weights, SaP operates post-hoc in the representation space, preserving model capabilities while enforcing safety constraints. Experiments across multiple LLMs demonstrate that our method can effectively detect unethical inputs, reduce adversarial attack success rates while maintaining performance on standard tasks, thus highlighting the importance of having an explicit geometric model for safety. Analysis of the learned polytope facets reveals emergence of specialization in detecting different semantic notions of safety, providing interpretable insights into how safety is captured in LLMs' representation space.

papers.title: To Steer or Not to Steer? Mechanistic Error Reduction with Abstention for Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we effectively steer language models to mitigate errors by calibrating when and how much to steer, thereby avoiding under- and oversteering?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces MERA, a principled framework for error mitigation in language models via calibrated activation steering, which optimizes intervention direction and strength to provably improve performance or abstain.
papers.conclusion: MERA provides a safe, effective, and general-purpose framework for mechanistic activation steering that guarantees improved or non-degrading performance through calibrated interventions.
papers.key_findings:
MERA outperforms existing steering baselines across diverse models and tasks, providing safe and non-degrading error correction.
Steering based on the 'exact' token position (first token matching a valid label) generally performs as well as or better than the traditional 'last' token position.
Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) features do not consistently improve probe performance for error estimation compared to original activations.
MERA can be applied on top of existing steering techniques (e.g., contrastive or probe-based) to further enhance their performance.
The calibration step in MERA ensures interventions are only applied when they are confidently beneficial, preventing performance degradation.
papers.limitation:
Evaluation is limited to multiple-choice question answering (MCQA) classification tasks, which may not reflect performance in more complex, open-ended generation tasks.
Steering for specialized error correction might inadvertently impair the model's general capabilities or text fluency.
future_direction: Extend MERA to alignment objectives such as toxicity reduction, refusal behavior, and harmfulness mitigation.
Replace linear error probes with non-linear estimators (e.g., neural networks).
Investigate the impact of using different evaluation metrics (e.g., F1 score) during calibration for tasks with class imbalance.
papers.abstract: We introduce Mechanistic Error Reduction with Abstention (MERA), a principled framework for steering language models (LMs) to mitigate errors through selective, adaptive interventions. Unlike existing methods that rely on fixed, manually tuned steering strengths, often resulting in under or oversteering, MERA addresses these limitations by (i) optimising the intervention direction, and (ii) calibrating when, and how much to steer, thereby provably improving performance or abstaining when no confident correction is possible. Experiments across diverse datasets, and LM families demonstrate safe, effective, non-degrading error correction, and that MERA outperforms existing baselines. Moreover, MERA can be applied on top of existing steering techniques to further enhance their performance, establishing it as a general-purpose, and efficient approach to mechanistic activation steering.

papers.title: Semantics-Adaptive Activation Intervention for LLMs via Dynamic Steering Vectors
papers.research_question: How can activation intervention methods be made adaptive to the semantic context of inputs, overcoming the limitation of fixed steering vectors?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes SADI, a dynamic activation intervention method that constructs a steering vector tailored to each input's semantic context, improving task performance without training and generalizing across various LLMs and tasks.
papers.conclusion: SADI advances activation engineering by providing a dynamic and adaptive intervention method that significantly improves model performance across diverse tasks and models without requiring training.
papers.key_findings:
SADI outperforms fixed steering baseline methods (ITI, CAA) by substantial margins across multiple-choice and open-ended generation tasks.
SADI is effective across different model backbones (LLAMA2, BLOOMZ, MISTRAL, FALCON) and model sizes (560M to 7B).
SADI works in few-shot and multilingual settings, demonstrating broad generalizability.
SADI requires only a small number of contrastive pairs (e.g., 150) and no training, making it cost-effective.
Interventions targeting attention heads (SADI-HEAD) consistently yield significant performance improvements across tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable performance across many tasks, yet aligning them with desired behaviors remains challenging. Activation intervention has emerged as an effective and economical method to modify the behavior of LLMs. Despite considerable interest in this area, current intervention methods exclusively employ a fixed steering vector to modify model activations, lacking adaptability to diverse input semantics. To address this limitation, we propose Semantics-Adaptive Dynamic Intervention (SADI), a novel method that constructs a dynamic steering vector to intervene model activations at inference time. More specifically, SADI utilizes activation differences in contrastive pairs to precisely identify critical elements of an LLM (i.e., attention heads, hidden states, and neurons) for targeted intervention. During inference, SADI dynamically steers model behavior by scaling element-wise activations based on the directions of input semantics. Experimental results show that SADI outperforms established baselines by substantial margins, improving task performance without training. SADI's cost-effectiveness and generalizability across various LLM backbones and tasks highlight its potential as a versatile alignment technique.

papers.title: Aligned Probing: Relating Toxic Behavior and Model Internals
papers.research_question: How do LMs encode information about toxicity, and what is the interplay between their internals and behavior?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces aligned probing, a framework to relate model behavior and internals for toxicity, and shows that LMs encode toxicity information strongly in lower layers, and that stronger encoding of input toxicity leads to less toxic output.
papers.conclusion: Aligned probing traces text properties from input to output, revealing that model behavior heavily relies on input toxicity, highlighting a dilemma: generating semantically relevant output without inheriting unwanted properties like toxicity.
papers.key_findings:
LMs encode information about toxicity strongly in lower layers.
LMs replicate and amplify toxicity more than humans, especially for attributes sensitive to single words.
Instruction-tuned models are less toxic and encode toxicity differently, with information more spread across layers.
Less toxic models encode more information about input toxicity.
Causal interventions show that skipping layers increases toxicity, indicating that information about input toxicity helps generate less toxic text.
papers.limitation:
Classifying toxicity is non-trivial due to conceptual variations, dataset differences, and contextual nature.
Generalization is limited to English and specific model families.
Computational costs for probing and interventions are high.
future_direction: Apply aligned probing to analyze other aspects of generation, like stereotypical formulations.
Examine the nature of other mitigation methods, such as model merging.
papers.abstract: We introduce aligned probing, a novel interpretability framework that aligns the behavior of language models (LMs), based on their outputs, and their internal representations (internals). Using this framework, we examine over 20 OLMo, Llama, and Mistral models, bridging behavioral and internal perspectives for toxicity for the first time. Our results show that LMs strongly encode information about the toxicity level of inputs and subsequent outputs, particularly in lower layers. Focusing on how unique LMs differ offers both correlative and causal evidence that they generate less toxic output when strongly encoding information about the input toxicity. We also highlight the heterogeneity of toxicity, as model behavior and internals vary across unique attributes such as Threat. Finally, four case studies analyzing detoxification, multi-prompt evaluations, model quantization, and pre-training dynamics underline the practical impact of aligned probing with further concrete insights. Our findings contribute to a more holistic understanding of LMs, both within and beyond the context of toxicity.

papers.title: The Straight and Narrow: Do LLMs Possess an Internal Moral Path?
papers.research_question: Do LLMs possess an internal moral path, or are they merely capturing superficial linguistic artifacts? The paper investigates the internal moral representations of LLMs and how to manipulate them for safety.
papers.core_contribution: The paper maps Moral Foundations Theory onto the latent space of LLMs, confirming linearly separable moral representations, and introduces Adaptive Moral Fusion (AMF) to dynamically steer these representations for safety, effectively balancing the safety-helpfulness trade-off.
papers.conclusion: The work bridges the gap between superficial behavioral guardrails and intrinsic alignment by mapping and manipulating moral representations within LLMs, demonstrating that activation engineering can serve as a robust intrinsic defense mechanism.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs encode linearly separable moral representations in their middle layers, forming a shared yet distinct moral subspace across English and Chinese.
Steerable Moral Vectors can be extracted and causally modulate the model's internal state and behavioral output, shifting responses between 'Virtue' and 'Vice'.
Adaptive Moral Fusion (AMF) synergizes probe detection with vector injection, reducing jailbreak success rates on HarmBench while minimizing incorrect refusals on XSTest.
Cross-lingual analysis reveals 'Asymmetric Feature Coverage' where some moral concepts (e.g., Care, Loyalty-Vice) are more richly encoded in Chinese, while others (e.g., Sanctity-Virtue, Authority-Virtue) are more robust in English.
Moral Vector injection reveals implicit correlations between foundations, such as Fairness and Loyalty amplifying Authority-virtue, and identifies Sanctity-vice as a 'universal negative pole'.
papers.limitation:
The cultural and theoretical scope is limited to English and Chinese and grounded solely in Moral Foundations Theory, potentially overlooking other ethical frameworks and low-resource cultures.
The Moral Virtue-Vice dataset was generated by an LLM (Gemini 3 Pro) without large-scale human annotation, potentially reflecting the generator's biases.
Validation was primarily on the Llama-3.1 family; generalizability to other architectures requires further study.
future_direction: Extending the framework to diverse model architectures.
Expanding the cross-lingual analysis to capture a broader spectrum of global cultural morality.
Incorporating ethical frameworks beyond Moral Foundations Theory.
papers.abstract: Enhancing the moral alignment of Large Language Models (LLMs) is a critical challenge in AI safety. Current alignment techniques often act as superficial guardrails, leaving the intrinsic moral representations of LLMs largely untouched. In this paper, we bridge this gap by leveraging Moral Foundations Theory (MFT) to map and manipulate the fine-grained moral landscape of LLMs. Through cross-lingual linear probing, we validate the shared nature of moral representations in middle layers and uncover a shared yet different moral subspace between English and Chinese. Building upon this, we extract steerable Moral Vectors and successfully validate their efficacy at both internal and behavioral levels. Leveraging the high generalizability of morality, we propose Adaptive Moral Fusion (AMF), a dynamic inference-time intervention that synergizes probe detection with vector injection to tackle the safety-helpfulness trade-off. Empirical results confirm that our approach acts as a targeted intrinsic defense, effectively reducing incorrect refusals on benign queries while minimizing jailbreak success rates compared to standard baselines.

papers.title: Controllable Safety Alignment: Inference-Time Adaptation to Diverse Safety Requirements
papers.research_question: How can we efficiently adjust model safety without re-training for each safety requirement?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Controllable Safety Alignment (CoSA), a framework for inference-time adaptation to diverse safety requirements without retraining, and introduces CoSAlign, a data-centric method to improve controllability.
papers.conclusion: CoSA framework allows models to adapt to diverse safety requirements at inference time, promoting pluralism in safety alignment and increasing practicality.
papers.key_findings:
CoSAlign significantly improves controllability over strong baselines including in-context alignment.
CoSAlign generalizes well to unseen safety configs.
In-context alignment is insufficient for complex safety configs due to difficulty in constructing high-quality demonstrations.
Models trained with CoSAlign balance helpfulness and configured safety as measured by CoSA-Score.
The framework enables pluralistic safety alignment, allowing models to serve diverse user needs.
papers.abstract: The current paradigm for safety alignment of large language models (LLMs) follows a one-size-fits-all approach: the model refuses to interact with any content deemed unsafe by the model provider. This approach lacks flexibility in the face of varying social norms across cultures and regions. In addition, users may have diverse safety needs, making a model with static safety standards too restrictive to be useful, as well as too costly to be re-aligned. We propose Controllable Safety Alignment (CoSA), a framework designed to adapt models to diverse safety requirements without re-training. Instead of aligning a fixed model, we align models to follow safety configs -- free-form natural language descriptions of the desired safety behaviors -- that are provided as part of the system prompt. To adjust model safety behavior, authorized users only need to modify such safety configs at inference time. To enable that, we propose CoSAlign, a data-centric method for aligning LLMs to easily adapt to diverse safety configs. Furthermore, we devise a novel controllability evaluation protocol that considers both helpfulness and configured safety, summarizing them into CoSA-Score, and construct CoSApien, a human-authored benchmark that consists of real-world LLM use cases with diverse safety requirements and corresponding evaluation prompts. We show that CoSAlign leads to substantial gains of controllability over strong baselines including in-context alignment. Our framework encourages better representation and adaptation to pluralistic human values in LLMs, and thereby increasing their practicality.

papers.title: Alignment Quality Index (AQI) : Beyond Refusals: AQI as an Intrinsic Alignment Diagnostic via Latent Geometry, Cluster Divergence, and Layer wise Pooled Representations
papers.research_question: How can we assess LLM alignment intrinsically by analyzing the separation of safe and unsafe activations in latent space? Which layers and geometric metrics best capture this alignment?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Alignment Quality Index (AQI), a decoding-invariant metric that assesses LLM alignment by measuring the separability of safe and unsafe activations in latent space, and the LITMUS dataset for robust evaluation.
papers.conclusion: AQI provides a decoding-invariant, representation-grounded metric for latent safety evaluation, offering a new lens into model cognition and a pathway for deeper alignment-aware auditing.
papers.key_findings:
AQI correlates with G-Eval and LLM judge scores, validating it as a proxy for alignment.
AQI detects jailbreak-induced representation collapse even when surface metrics show compliance.
AQI reveals alignment drift under safety-agnostic fine-tuning before output metrics degrade.
AQI remains stable across decoding temperatures, unlike behavioral metrics.
AQI can diagnose alignment faking by measuring train-test divergence in latent space.
papers.limitation: AQI relies on the assumption that alignment is reflected in latent geometry, which may not hold for all models or failure modes.
future_direction: Extending AQI to multimodal models and other architectures.
Integrating AQI with causal attribution methods for interpretable diagnostics.
Developing automated alignment auditing pipelines using AQI.
papers.abstract: Abhilekh Borah, Chhavi Sharma, Danush Khanna, Utkarsh Bhatt, Gurpreet Singh, Hasnat Md Abdullah, Raghav Kaushik Ravi, Vinija Jain, Jyoti Patel, Shubham Singh, Vasu Sharma, Arpita Vats, Rahul Raja, Aman Chadha, Amitava Das. Proceedings of the 2025 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing. 2025.

papers.title: What Makes and Breaks Safety Fine-tuning? A Mechanistic Study
papers.research_question: What is the safety mechanism learned by the model via safety fine-tuning, and how are jailbreak and adversarial attacks able to bypass this mechanism?
papers.core_contribution: Safety fine-tuning methods minimally transform MLP weights to project unsafe inputs into the null space, causing clustering of safe and unsafe activations; jailbreaks bypass safety by having activations similar to safe samples.
papers.conclusion: Safety fine-tuning minimally transforms MLP weights to project unsafe inputs into the null space, leading to clustering; jailbreaks bypass this by having activations similar to safe samples. This mechanistic understanding can inform more robust safety fine-tuning.
papers.key_findings:
Safety fine-tuning leads to separate clusters of activations for safe and unsafe samples.
The transformation ∆W has its column-space aligned with the null-space of the instruction fine-tuned weights, making it orthogonal to the original weights.
∆W preferentially impacts unsafe samples, as their pre-activations have larger projection onto the row-space of ∆W.
The local Lipschitzness of the model decreases for unsafe samples after safety fine-tuning, making the model less sensitive to perturbations on unsafe inputs.
Jailbreak attacks (competing objectives, mismatched generalization, adversarial embeddings) have activations that are closer to safe samples, thus bypassing the safety mechanism.
future_direction: Using ∆W from stronger safety fine-tuning methods to improve weaker ones
Designing more robust safety fine-tuning protocols based on the mechanistic understanding
papers.abstract: Safety fine-tuning helps align Large Language Models (LLMs) with human preferences for their safe deployment. To better understand the underlying factors that make models safe via safety fine-tuning, we design a synthetic data generation framework that captures salient aspects of an unsafe input by modeling the interaction between the task the model is asked to perform (e.g., "design") versus the specific concepts the task is asked to be performed upon (e.g., a "cycle" vs. a "bomb"). Using this, we investigate three well-known safety fine-tuning methods -- supervised safety fine-tuning, direct preference optimization, and unlearning -- and provide significant evidence demonstrating that these methods minimally transform MLP weights to specifically align unsafe inputs into its weights' null space. This yields a clustering of inputs based on whether the model deems them safe or not. Correspondingly, when an adversarial input (e.g., a jailbreak) is provided, its activations are closer to safer samples, leading to the model processing such an input as if it were safe. We validate our findings, wherever possible, on real-world models -- specifically, Llama-2 7B and Llama-3 8B.

papers.title: Mechanistic understanding and validation of large AI models with SemanticLens
papers.research_question: How can we achieve automated explanation and validation of model components at scale to understand their inner knowledge and ensure alignment with human expectations?
papers.core_contribution: SemanticLens is a universal explanation method that embeds neural network components into the semantic space of a foundation model, enabling scalable search, description, comparison, and auditing of learned concepts for component-level understanding and validation.
papers.conclusion: By enabling component-level understanding and validation, SemanticLens helps mitigate the opacity of AI models, facilitating more reliable deployment in critical applications.
papers.key_findings:
SemanticLens enables text-based search to identify neurons encoding specific concepts, such as biases or data artefacts, in models like ResNet50v2.
It can describe and structure the internal knowledge of models through semantic embeddings, revealing clusters of concepts like animals and vehicles.
The method allows auditing of concept alignment with expected reasoning, detecting spurious correlations and measuring reliance on valid vs. spurious concepts.
In medical image analysis, SemanticLens identifies spurious components (e.g., scale bars, band-aids) and enables model correction via pruning or retraining, improving robustness.
It introduces interpretability measures (clarity, polysemanticity, redundancy) that correlate with human perception and vary across architectures and training regimes.
papers.limitation: Concepts may be distributed across several components, and the neural basis may not comprehensively capture all relevant concepts.
papers.abstract: Abstract Unlike human-engineered systems, such as aeroplanes, for which the role and dependencies of each component are well understood, the inner workings of artificial intelligence models remain largely opaque, which hinders verifiability and undermines trust. Current approaches to neural network interpretability, including input attribution methods, probe-based analysis and activation visualization techniques, typically provide limited insights about the role of individual components or require extensive manual interpretation that cannot scale with model complexity. This paper introduces SemanticLens, a universal explanation method for neural networks that maps hidden knowledge encoded by components (for example, individual neurons) into the semantically structured, multimodal space of a foundation model such as CLIP. In this space, unique operations become possible, including (1) textual searches to identify neurons encoding specific concepts, (2) systematic analysis and comparison of model representations, (3) automated labelling of neurons and explanation of their functional roles, and (4) audits to validate decision-making against requirements. Fully scalable and operating without human input, SemanticLens is shown to be effective for debugging and validation, summarizing model knowledge, aligning reasoning with expectations (for example, adherence to the ABCDE rule in melanoma classification) and detecting components tied to spurious correlations and their associated training data. By enabling component-level understanding and validation, the proposed approach helps mitigate the opacity that limits confidence in artificial intelligence systems compared to traditional engineered systems, enabling more reliable deployment in critical applications.

papers.title: Advancing LLM Safe Alignment with Safety Representation Ranking
papers.research_question: How can we improve LLM safety by leveraging internal representations to rank candidate responses without altering the model's decoding logic?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Safety Representation Ranking (SRR), a listwise ranking framework that uses LLM internal representations to rank candidate responses by safety, without altering the model's decoding logic, improving robustness to adversarial prompts.
papers.conclusion: SRR serves as a practical and effective safeguard module for LLM alignment, offering a new paradigm for enhancing the safety and reliability of LLMs in real-world applications.
papers.key_findings:
SRR significantly improves robustness to adversarial prompts across multiple benchmarks.
SRR generalizes well across different safety evaluation datasets.
SRR can be adapted to other alignment perspectives like privacy and fairness.
SRR maintains natural performance on benign tasks (e.g., mathematical reasoning).
SRR outperforms baseline reward models in safety ranking accuracy despite being much smaller.
papers.limitation:
SRR might need task-specific fine-tuning for optimal performance in certain situations.
SRR's adaptability to special-domain safety scenarios requires further testing.
SRR's effectiveness relies on the LLM generating diverse candidate responses; if responses lack diversity, performance may be affected.
papers.abstract: The rapid advancement of large language models (LLMs) has demonstrated milestone success in a variety of tasks, yet their potential for generating harmful content has raised significant safety concerns. Existing safety evaluation approaches typically operate directly on textual responses, overlooking the rich information embedded in the model's internal representations. In this paper, we propose Safety Representation Ranking (SRR), a listwise ranking framework that selects safe responses using hidden states from the LLM itself. SRR encodes both instructions and candidate completions using intermediate transformer representations and ranks candidates via a lightweight similarity-based scorer. Our approach directly leverages internal model states and supervision at the list level to capture subtle safety signals. Experiments across multiple benchmarks show that SRR significantly improves robustness to adversarial prompts. Our code will be available upon publication.

papers.title: Light Alignment Improves LLM Safety via Model Self-Reflection with a Single Neuron
papers.research_question: How can we design a lightweight safety alignment method that uses a single neuron as a gating mechanism to balance model intrinsic capabilities and external guidance, thereby improving safety without compromising utility?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a lightweight safety alignment method (NGSD) that uses a single neuron as a gating mechanism to balance intrinsic model capabilities with external safety guidance, achieving a favorable safety-utility trade-off with minimal training overhead.
papers.conclusion: Lightweight and targeted safety alignment mechanisms, such as NGSD, can provide meaningful safety improvements without significantly degrading utility, offering a practical direction for deploying safer large language models.
papers.key_findings:
NGSD reduces attack success rates across multiple jailbreak attack scenarios (e.g., GCG, PAIR, AutoDAN).
NGSD preserves utility on benign tasks (e.g., GSM8K, Just-Eval) better than strong baselines like SafeDecoding.
The neuron-based gating mechanism is more robust and responsive than alternative gating methods (EMA, SMG).
The method demonstrates strong generalization and transferability across model scales and families.
NGSD requires only training a small expert model and efficiently transfers to larger models within the same family.
papers.limitation:
Effectiveness in more open-ended or long-horizon settings remains unclear.
Differences in tokenization limit generalization across model families.
future_direction: Explore adaptive risk estimation and more general safety alignment strategies.
Conduct cross-family evaluation under diverse generation regimes.
papers.abstract: The safety of large language models (LLMs) has increasingly emerged as a fundamental aspect of their development. Existing safety alignment for LLMs is predominantly achieved through post-training methods, which are computationally expensive and often fail to generalize well across different models. A small number of lightweight alignment approaches either rely heavily on prior-computed safety injections or depend excessively on the model's own capabilities, resulting in limited generalization and degraded efficiency and usability during generation. In this work, we propose a safety-aware decoding method that requires only low-cost training of an expert model and employs a single neuron as a gating mechanism. By effectively balancing the model's intrinsic capabilities with external guidance, our approach simultaneously preserves utility and enhances output safety. It demonstrates clear advantages in training overhead and generalization across model scales, offering a new perspective on lightweight alignment for the safe and practical deployment of large language models. Code: https://github.com/Beijing-AISI/NGSD.

papers.title: Enhancing Multiple Dimensions of Trustworthiness in LLMs via Sparse Activation Control
papers.research_question: How can we enhance multiple dimensions of trustworthiness (safety, factuality, bias) in LLMs simultaneously without training, by controlling sparse activations in specific model components?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Sparse Activation Control, a training-free method that enhances multiple trustworthiness dimensions in LLMs by identifying sparse, task-specific attention heads and controlling their representations using Gaussian Mixture Models, avoiding control conflicts.
papers.conclusion: Sparse Activation Control is an effective training-free method for enhancing multi-dimensional trustworthiness in LLMs by leveraging sparse and independent task-specific components.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse Activation Control can enhance safety, factuality, and bias simultaneously without significant interference, outperforming representation engineering baselines in multi-task control.
Attention heads for different tasks are sparse and have minimal overlap, allowing independent control.
The method does not significantly harm general model performance on MMLU and CSQA.
The method generalizes to other models (Qwen series) and additional trustworthiness tasks (robustness, privacy).
Control shifts head outputs towards task-relevant tokens, as shown by unembedding projections.
papers.limitation:
Relies on construction of paired stimuli, which may require domain knowledge.
Experiments are limited to a few models and tasks.
future_direction: Extend to more tasks and models
Explore theoretical foundations of sparsity
papers.abstract: As the development and application of Large Language Models (LLMs) continue to advance rapidly, enhancing their trustworthiness and aligning them with human preferences has become a critical area of research. Traditional methods rely heavily on extensive data for Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF), but representation engineering offers a new, training-free approach. This technique leverages semantic features to control the representation of LLM's intermediate hidden states, enabling the model to meet specific requirements such as increased honesty or heightened safety awareness. However, a significant challenge arises when attempting to fulfill multiple requirements simultaneously. It proves difficult to encode various semantic contents, like honesty and safety, into a singular semantic feature, restricting its practicality. In this work, we address this issue through ``Sparse Activation Control''. By delving into the intrinsic mechanisms of LLMs, we manage to identify and pinpoint components that are closely related to specific tasks within the model, i.e., attention heads. These heads display sparse characteristics that allow for near-independent control over different tasks. Our experiments, conducted on the open-source Llama series models, have yielded encouraging results. The models were able to align with human preferences on issues of safety, factuality, and bias concurrently.

papers.title: Mind the Inconspicuous: Revealing the Hidden Weakness in Aligned LLMs' Refusal Boundaries
papers.research_question: How can appending end-of-sequence (eos) tokens bypass the learned refusal boundary in aligned LLMs, and what is the underlying mechanism of 'context segmentation'?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reveals the 'context segmentation' phenomenon where appending eos tokens shifts prompts towards the refusal boundary in hidden space, and introduces BOOST, a simple method to enhance jailbreak attacks by appending eos tokens.
papers.conclusion: The work highlights a critical blind spot in LLM alignment and content filtering, urging the community to address the security implications of control tokens and develop more robust refusal boundaries.
papers.key_findings:
Appending multiple eos tokens causes both harmful and benign prompts to shift toward the learned refusal boundary in the hidden representation space, a phenomenon termed 'context segmentation'.
BOOST significantly increases the attack success rate (ASR) of existing jailbreak techniques across a wide range of open-source LLMs.
Commercial LLM APIs (OpenAI, Anthropic, Qwen) do not filter eos tokens, making them vulnerable to BOOST-enhanced attacks.
eos tokens have low attention values, minimizing distraction from the harmful content and preserving jailbreak effectiveness.
BOOST can be made more robust to simple filtering through eos token obfuscation and dynamic positioning strategies.
future_direction: Implement input-filtering defenses for control tokens like eos.
Develop more robust and generalizable refusal boundaries to defend against context segmentation attacks.
Investigate the security impact of all control tokens and develop comprehensive defense strategies.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) have led to impressive alignment where models learn to distinguish harmful from harmless queries through supervised finetuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF). In this paper, we reveal a subtle yet impactful weakness in these aligned models. We find that simply appending multiple end of sequence (eos) tokens can cause a phenomenon we call context segmentation, which effectively shifts both harmful and benign inputs closer to the refusal boundary in the hidden space. Building on this observation, we propose a straightforward method to BOOST jailbreak attacks by appending eos tokens. Our systematic evaluation shows that this strategy significantly increases the attack success rate across 8 representative jailbreak techniques and 16 open-source LLMs, ranging from 2B to 72B parameters. Moreover, we develop a novel probing mechanism for commercial APIs and discover that major providers such as OpenAI, Anthropic, and Qwen do not filter eos tokens, making them similarly vulnerable. These findings highlight a hidden yet critical blind spot in existing alignment and content filtering approaches. We call for heightened attention to eos tokens' unintended influence on model behaviors, particularly in production systems. Our work not only calls for an input-filtering based defense, but also points to new defenses that make refusal boundaries more robust and generalizable, as well as fundamental alignment techniques that can defend against context segmentation attacks.

papers.title: Multi-Level Safety Continual Projection for Fine-Tuned Large Language Models without Retraining
papers.research_question: How to achieve robust safety alignment in fine-tuned LLMs with minimal parameter changes and without retraining, while maintaining utility and allowing continual adaptation to emerging safety concerns?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes MSCP, a training-free post-fine-tuning safety enhancement method that identifies sparse safety-critical neurons via multi-level representations and applies safety-direction projections to suppress harmful outputs with minimal parameter changes, preserving utility and enabling continual adaptation.
papers.conclusion: MSCP effectively enhances safety in fine-tuned LLMs with minimal parameter changes and no retraining, enabling continual adaptation and preserving utility, highlighting the value of fine-grained model introspection for scalable safety defenses.
papers.key_findings:
MSCP reduces harmfulness scores and attack success rates with minimal parameter edits (e.g., 4.67% for Qwen) while preserving model utility.
MSCP achieves continual safety improvement across multiple risk dimensions, with decreasing parameter changes for new dimensions (e.g., 0.73% for Terrorism).
Ablation shows that safety layers at one-third model depth (layers 10-15) yield the best safety and utility balance.
papers.limitation: The ability to continual learning across more complex and diverse safety dimensions remains an area for further investigation.
papers.abstract: While fine-tuning services drive the rapid expansion of task capabilities in large language models (LLMs), they are often accompanied by the degradation and reorganization of safety-aligned representations, making models more prone to deviating from human preferences and exposing them to emerging jailbreak risks. Existing post-fine-tuning defense methods predominantly rely on single-scale safety correction mechanisms, which struggle to achieve a robust balance among safety, model utility, and continual adaptability. We propose Multi-Level Safety Continual Projection (MSCP), a training-free post-fine-tuning safety enhancement method that implicitly aligns global and localized safety activations through coordinated multi-level representations to isolate sparse neuron clusters governing safety-sensitive behaviors. It then applies composable safety-direction projections without retraining, effectively suppressing harmful outputs under minimal parameter perturbations while preserving task performance and improving alignment with human preferences. Extensive experiments across multiple fine-tuned LLM models demonstrate that our method significantly reduce harmfulness scores and attack success rates with minimal parameter modifications, while preserving the model's utility. Furthermore, we introduce a task-specific, multi-dimensional heterogeneous safety activation clustering mechanism that enables continual defense and generalization capability against unforeseen emerging safety concerns.

papers.title: Navigating the OverKill in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What factors contribute to overkill (excessive refusal to answer benign queries) in large language models, and how can it be mitigated?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces Self-Contrastive Decoding (Self-CD), a training-free and model-agnostic method that reduces overkill in LLMs by mitigating shortcuts in attention to harmful words, achieving lower refusal rates without compromising safety.
papers.conclusion: The paper defines overkill in LLMs and proposes Self-CD, a simple and effective method that significantly reduces refusal rates without training, addressing shortcuts in model attention.
papers.key_findings:
Models exhibit shortcuts, leading to over-attention to harmful words like 'kill', regardless of query semantics.
Safety-emphasized system prompts exacerbate overkill by increasing reliance on shortcuts.
Self-CD reduces refusal rates by an average of 20% across models while maintaining safety.
Overkill is widespread across various models, independent of size or architecture.
Models have a superficial understanding of user queries, relying on word-level cues rather than full semantics.
papers.limitation: Incomplete availability of training data for large models limits further research.
future_direction: Analyze biases or toxicity in human feedback datasets.
Investigate shortcuts or misgeneralizations in reward models.
papers.abstract: Large language models are meticulously aligned to be both helpful and harmless. However, recent research points to a potential overkill which means models may refuse to answer benign queries. In this paper, we investigate the factors for overkill by exploring how models handle and determine the safety of queries. Our findings reveal the presence of shortcuts within models, leading to an over-attention of harmful words like 'kill' and prompts emphasizing safety will exacerbate overkill. Based on these insights, we introduce Self-Contrastive Decoding (Self-CD), a training-free and model-agnostic strategy, to alleviate this phenomenon. We first extract such over-attention by amplifying the difference in the model's output distributions when responding to system prompts that either include or omit an emphasis on safety. Then we determine the final next-token predictions by downplaying the over-attention from the model via contrastive decoding. Empirical results indicate that our method has achieved an average reduction of the refusal rate by 20\% while having almost no impact on safety.

papers.title: Representation Bending for Large Language Model Safety
papers.research_question: How can we enhance LLM safety by bending the representation space to separate safe and unsafe representations, bringing activation steering to fine-tuning?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces REPBEND, a method that brings activation steering to fine-tuning by bending the representation space to separate safe and unsafe representations, achieving state-of-the-art safety performance with minimal impact on general capabilities.
papers.conclusion: REPBEND effectively enhances LLM safety by bending representations to separate safe and unsafe states, achieving state-of-the-art performance with minimal impact on general capabilities, offering a scalable safety solution.
papers.key_findings:
REPBEND achieves up to 95% reduction in attack success rates across diverse jailbreak benchmarks.
REPBEND maintains general capabilities and usability, with minimal degradation on standard benchmarks.
REPBEND outperforms prior methods such as Circuit Breaker, RMU, and NPO in both black-box and white-box attacks.
REPBEND works best when applied to mid-to-later layers of the transformer.
REPBEND's loss function, which includes L2 norm, cosine similarity, and KL divergence terms, effectively separates safe and unsafe representations.
papers.limitation:
REPBEND requires a dataset of safe and unsafe prompts, which may not cover all possible harmful scenarios.
The method relies on the choice of layers and hyperparameters, which may need tuning for different models.
The transferability of LoRA for safety improvements remains an open challenge.
future_direction: Exploring the transferability of LoRA adapters for safety across models.
Extending REPBEND to multimodal settings.
Investigating the theoretical foundations of representation bending.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have emerged as powerful tools, but their inherent safety risks - ranging from harmful content generation to broader societal harms - pose significant challenges. These risks can be amplified by the recent adversarial attacks, fine-tuning vulnerabilities, and the increasing deployment of LLMs in high-stakes environments. Existing safety-enhancing techniques, such as fine-tuning with human feedback or adversarial training, are still vulnerable as they address specific threats and often fail to generalize across unseen attacks, or require manual system-level defenses. This paper introduces RepBend, a novel approach that fundamentally disrupts the representations underlying harmful behaviors in LLMs, offering a scalable solution to enhance (potentially inherent) safety. RepBend brings the idea of activation steering - simple vector arithmetic for steering model's behavior during inference - to loss-based fine-tuning. Through extensive evaluation, RepBend achieves state-of-the-art performance, outperforming prior methods such as Circuit Breaker, RMU, and NPO, with up to 95% reduction in attack success rates across diverse jailbreak benchmarks, all with negligible reduction in model usability and general capabilities.

papers.title: Self-correction is Not An Innate Capability in Language Models
papers.research_question: Is moral self-correction an innate capability of Large Language Models (LLMs)?
papers.core_contribution: Moral self-correction is not an inherent capability of LLMs, as they lack moral sensitivity and cannot effectively incorporate external feedback during the self-correction process.
papers.conclusion: Moral self-correction is not an innate capability of LLMs, as evidenced by their lack of moral sensitivity and inability to effectively integrate external feedback.
papers.key_findings:
Self-correction does not enhance LLMs' moral sensitivity in most evaluated scenarios.
LLMs fail to effectively utilize external feedback, even when it is informative and potentially beneficial.
External feedback exhibits non-positive effects on Chain-of-Thought (CoT), often reducing the activation of warrants within the CoT.
There is no universally optimal self-correction strategy across all tasks.
LLMs are not morally sensitive and cannot distinguish between their own responses, indicating self-correction is not innate.
papers.abstract: Although there has been growing interest in the self-correction capability of Large Language Models (LLMs), there are varying conclusions about its effectiveness. Prior research has largely concentrated on intrinsic self-correction, extrinsic self-correction, particularly the interplay between internal knowledge and external feedback, remains underexplored. In this paper, we aim to comprehensively investigate the underlying mechanism of moral self-correction by addressing a fundamental question: is moral self-correction an innate capability of LLMs? Specifically, we conduct: (1) a behavioral analysis of LLMs' moral sensitivity based on a self-distinguishing task; and (2) a mechanistic analysis of the hidden states to examine how key components of self-correction, such as Chain-of-Thought (CoT) and external feedback, interact to facilitate moral self-correction. Drawing on empirical evidence from both behavioral and mechanistic analyses, we demonstrate that moral self-correction is not an inherent capability of LLMs, as they are neither morally sensitive nor able to effectively incorporate external feedback during the self-correction process.

papers.title: A Guardrail for Safety Preservation: When Safety-Sensitive Subspace Meets Harmful-Resistant Null-Space
papers.research_question: How to preserve safety alignment of large language models during fine-tuning on downstream tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes GuardSpace, a framework that initializes low-rank adapters in a safety-irrelevant subspace and constrains their updates to a harmful-resistant null space, preserving safety alignment during fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: GuardSpace effectively preserves safety alignment during fine-tuning, achieving state-of-the-art trade-off between safety and downstream task performance.
papers.key_findings:
GuardSpace achieves lower harmful score and higher fine-tuning accuracy compared to state-of-the-art methods like AsFT.
GuardSpace maintains low harmful score across different model architectures (Llama-2, Qwen-2, Gemma-2).
GuardSpace is robust to varying proportions of unsafe examples in the fine-tuning data.
The safety-sensitive subspace initialization and harmful-resistant null space projector are both effective components.
The method requires only a few hundred harmful prompts to construct an effective null space projector.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable success in diverse tasks, yet their safety alignment remains fragile during adaptation. Even when fine-tuning on benign data or with low-rank adaptation, pre-trained safety behaviors are easily degraded, leading to harmful responses in the fine-tuned models. To address this challenge, we propose GuardSpace, a guardrail framework for preserving safety alignment throughout fine-tuning, composed of two key components: a safety-sensitive subspace and a harmful-resistant null space. First, we explicitly decompose pre-trained weights into safety-relevant and safety-irrelevant components using covariance-preconditioned singular value decomposition, and initialize low-rank adapters from the safety-irrelevant ones, while freezing safety-relevant components to preserve their associated safety mechanism. Second, we construct a null space projector that restricts adapter updates from altering safe outputs on harmful prompts, thereby maintaining the original refusal behavior. Experiments with various pre-trained models on multiple downstream tasks demonstrate that GuardSpace achieves superior performance over existing methods. Notably, for Llama-2-7B-Chat fine-tuned on GSM8K, GuardSpace outperforms the state-of-the-art method AsFT, reducing the average harmful score from 14.4% to 3.6%, while improving the accuracy from from 26.0% to 28.0%.

papers.title: Self-Detoxifying Language Models via Toxification Reversal
papers.research_question: How can pretrained language models be detoxified without fine-tuning or additional components by identifying and reversing the toxification direction in attention layers?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a lightweight method for language model detoxification that reverses the toxification direction in attention layers without fine-tuning, achieving comparable performance to state-of-the-art methods.
papers.conclusion: The method effectively detoxifies language models by manipulating attention layer information flow, providing a lightweight alternative to fine-tuning-based approaches.
papers.key_findings:
The method reduces toxicity effectively without fine-tuning, matching state-of-the-art performance.
Human evaluation shows it generates less toxic content while maintaining fluency and coherence.
Layer-wise ablation indicates that middle-upper attention layers are more critical for detoxification.
Adaptive scaling factors based on vector norms and similarities improve detoxification adaptability.
Logit lens analysis demonstrates suppression of toxic token probabilities in the residual stream.
papers.limitation:
The method's effectiveness depends on the model's pre-training knowledge and may not remove harmful content not associated with the prefix.
Full model access is required, making it unsuitable for API-only models.
papers.abstract: Language model detoxification aims to minimize the risk of generating offensive or harmful content in pretrained language models (PLMs) for safer deployment. Existing methods can be roughly categorized as finetuning-based and decoding-based. However, the former is often resource-intensive, while the latter relies on additional components and potentially compromises the generation fluency. In this paper, we propose a more lightweight approach that enables the PLM itself to achieve "self-detoxification". Our method is built upon the observation that prepending a negative steering prompt can effectively induce PLMs to generate toxic content. At the same time, we are inspired by the recent research in the interpretability field, which formulates the evolving contextualized representations within the PLM as an information stream facilitated by the attention layers. Drawing on this idea, we devise a method to identify the toxification direction from the normal generation process to the one prompted with the negative prefix, and then steer the generation to the reversed direction by manipulating the information movement within the attention layers. Experimental results show that our approach, without any fine-tuning or extra components, can achieve comparable performance with state-of-the-art methods.

papers.title: Can You Trust an LLM with Your Life-Changing Decision? An Investigation into AI High-Stakes Responses
papers.research_question: How do different LLMs respond to high-stakes queries, and how susceptible are they to sycophancy and overconfidence? Can their cautiousness be controlled via activation steering?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that LLMs vary in sycophancy and safety when giving high-stakes advice, with some models being more robust. It also demonstrates that activation steering can control cautiousness, suggesting a new path for safety alignment.
papers.conclusion: The study highlights the need for nuanced safety benchmarks for high-stakes advice and shows that activation steering can control model behavior, offering a path for improved alignment.
papers.key_findings:
Models vary in their susceptibility to sycophancy and overconfidence under user pressure, with some like o4-mini being more stable.
Top-performing models achieve high safety scores by frequently asking clarifying questions, indicating a safe, inquisitive approach.
Activation steering using a 'high-stakes' direction can reliably shift a model's tone and response framing, making it more cautious or more directive.
There is a tension between robustness, helpfulness, and cautiousness in model safety, indicating that safety is not monolithic.
The LLM Judge safety framework reveals that models can exhibit both safe and unsafe behaviors in the same response.
papers.limitation:
The scenarios were presented in a single turn, which may not capture the complexity of real multi-turn conversations.
The LLM Judge evaluations are not a substitute for human domain experts.
future_direction: Standardized benchmarks to evaluate performance on high-stakes advice tasks.
Using mechanistic interpretability and techniques like Pinpoint Tuning for safety alignment.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly consulted for high-stakes life advice, yet they lack standard safeguards against providing confident but misguided responses. This creates risks of sycophancy and over-confidence. This paper investigates these failure modes through three experiments: (1) a multiple-choice evaluation to measure model stability against user pressure; (2) a free-response analysis using a novel safety typology and an LLM Judge; and (3) a mechanistic interpretability experiment to steer model behavior by manipulating a "high-stakes" activation vector. Our results show that while some models exhibit sycophancy, others like o4-mini remain robust. Top-performing models achieve high safety scores by frequently asking clarifying questions, a key feature of a safe, inquisitive approach, rather than issuing prescriptive advice. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a model's cautiousness can be directly controlled via activation steering, suggesting a new path for safety alignment. These findings underscore the need for nuanced, multi-faceted benchmarks to ensure LLMs can be trusted with life-changing decisions.

papers.title: Angular Steering: Behavior Control via Rotation in Activation Space
papers.research_question: How can we control specific behaviors in large language models while preserving their general capabilities?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Angular Steering, a rotation-based framework for fine-grained behavior control in LLMs that generalizes existing activation steering methods and maintains general language modeling performance.
papers.conclusion: Angular Steering offers a principled, flexible, and robust framework for behavior control in LLMs, enabling fine-grained modulation while preserving general capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Angular Steering provides continuous, fine-grained control over behaviors like refusal and compliance by rotating activations in a fixed 2D subspace.
The method generalizes existing activation addition and directional ablation techniques under a unified geometric rotation framework.
Angular Steering maintains general language modeling performance (e.g., on TINYBENCHMARKS) while effectively steering behavior.
Adaptive Angular Steering, a selective variant, improves robustness and coherence by rotating only activations aligned with the target feature.
Experiments across multiple model families and sizes show the method's flexibility, generalization, and robustness compared to prior approaches.
papers.limitation: The method requires a contrastive dataset to extract the feature direction, which may not always be available.
future_direction: Extending Angular Steering to multi-feature steering and dynamic plane selection.
papers.abstract: Controlling specific behaviors in large language models while preserving their general capabilities is a central challenge for safe and reliable artificial intelligence deployment. Current steering methods, such as vector addition and directional ablation, are constrained within a two-dimensional subspace defined by the activation and feature direction, making them sensitive to chosen parameters and potentially affecting unrelated features due to unintended interactions in activation space. We introduce Angular Steering, a novel and flexible method for behavior modulation that operates by rotating activations within a fixed two-dimensional subspace. By formulating steering as a geometric rotation toward or away from a target behavior direction, Angular Steering provides continuous, fine-grained control over behaviors such as refusal and compliance. We demonstrate this method using refusal steering emotion steering as use cases. Additionally, we propose Adaptive Angular Steering, a selective variant that rotates only activations aligned with the target feature, further enhancing stability and coherence. Angular Steering generalizes existing addition and orthogonalization techniques under a unified geometric rotation framework, simplifying parameter selection and maintaining model stability across a broader range of adjustments. Experiments across multiple model families and sizes show that Angular Steering achieves robust behavioral control while maintaining general language modeling performance, underscoring its flexibility, generalization, and robustness compared to prior approaches. Code and artifacts are available at https://github.com/lone17/angular-steering/.

papers.title: Representation Surgery: Theory and Practice of Affine Steering
